title: Before the flood: what actually existed before 7 October 2023 - infrastructure, raw material, narratives, and the speed inference
question: To what extent were the distribution infrastructure, the networks and the narratives that spread false information after 7 October 2023 already existing, active or prepared before that date - and what exactly can be shown for each of the four separate claims folded into that question?
scope: Desk research over published platform takedown reports, research-institute analyses, government sanctions records, established fact-checks and investigative reporting, retrieved and archive-verified on 2026-08-27. The compound claim under test is split into four claims with different evidentiary bars: (1) distribution infrastructure existed and was active before 7 October 2023; (2) old material was recycled as raw material immediately after; (3) specific narratives were formulated or prepared in advance; (4) the speed of activation after 7 October implies prior coordination. Explicitly out of scope: any question of responsibility for the 7 October attack itself. This file assesses information infrastructure and narratives only.
publicInterestBasis: A version of the compound claim - that the lies about the war were prepared before it began - circulates widely, including in framings this site itself considers publishing. Establishing which parts of that claim the public record supports, at which grade, and which parts it does not, bears directly on public understanding of the post-7 October information environment and on this site's own accuracy. A claim of advance preparation that overstates its evidence would commit the exact fallacy this section documents in others.
confidence: **Confidence: high** that substantial distribution infrastructure and the recycled-material technique predate 7 October 2023; **low** on advance preparation of specific narratives, which the public record reviewed here does not establish; the speed-implies-coordination reading is an inference and is graded as one throughout.

bottomLine.text: **Claim 1 - pre-existing distribution infrastructure: documented.** Several of the networks that carried Israel-Hamas falsehoods after 7 October 2023 are documented as built and active well before it: the Doppelganger media-cloning operation from at least May 2022 (exposed publicly on 27 September 2022), the Spamouflage network active since 2019 with Meta's largest-ever single takedown announced 29 August 2023, Iranian content-laundering websites (IUVM) documented since 2018, and the Hamas-aligned Gaza Now channel with financial traces from August 2021. Each rests on a platform, government or research-institute record that predates the war or is independent of it.

bottomLine.text: **The same infrastructure demonstrably carried conflict content after 7 October.** ISD documented a pro-Kremlin ad network consistent with Doppelganger pushing Israel-Hamas narratives at French and German audiences, and Spamouflage assets folding the conflict into anti-US content; Microsoft documented a surge of Iranian cyber-enabled influence operations in support of Hamas. What predates the attack is the machinery. The conflict content itself appears on that machinery only after 7 October - none of these records shows war-specific material staged on it beforehand.

bottomLine.text: **Claim 2 - recycled raw material: documented, and the technique itself predates the war.** Within days of the attack, fact-checkers traced viral combat footage to the Arma 3 video game; the game's developer had already published a statement in November 2022 asking people to stop passing its footage off as real war video, after earlier misuse covering Afghanistan, Syria, Ukraine and prior Israel-Palestine escalations. The recycling technique required no preparation for this war because it was already routine practice with a documented history.

bottomLine.text: **Claim 3 - specific narratives prepared in advance: not established.** This desk searched for dated primary material showing any specific post-7 October false claim drafted, seeded or scheduled before the attack - and found none in the takedown reports, research-institute analyses and fact-check corpora reviewed. What is documented instead is the reuse of pre-existing narrative templates: the false-flag and denial repertoire, which long predates 7 October and attached to the event within days, and state-content laundering frames documented since 2018. A template is not a script. The distinction between an old repertoire being reused and a specific lie being pre-written is the central finding of this file.

bottomLine.text: **Claim 4 - speed as proof of advance coordination: an inference, and a contested one.** Cyabra reported roughly 40,000 fake pro-Hamas profiles in the first days of the war, stating that the fake profiles were created beforehand, some over a year earlier, and made active only when the war started - an activation pattern consistent with pre-positioning. But the strongest independent evidence cuts the other way: Microsoft found Iranian operators reactive and disorganized in the first days, re-using dated material, in a way indicating little or no coordination with Hamas; and NewsGuard found 74 percent of the most-viral false or unverified week-one posts on X came from paid-verified accounts - largely authentic, engagement-driven spread rather than covert networks. Speed and dormancy are observations; coordination is an inference from them, and this file grades it as an inference throughout.

limitations: Desk research only: this file synthesizes published platform reports, sanctions records, research-institute analyses and fact-checks. The desk ran no original network collection for this case, so it inherits each source's methodology and blind spots.

Commercial-firm findings (Cyabra, NewsGuard) rest on proprietary methods and samples that cannot be independently re-run from public data; both are therefore capped at medium reliability here regardless of how widely they were reported.

Scope excludes responsibility for the 7 October attack itself. Reporting on Hamas's pre-attack operational deception exists but concerns the attack, not post-attack false narratives, and is deliberately not used here.

Prevalence is unmeasured: no comprehensive study apportions post-7 October false content between pre-existing covert infrastructure and authentic engagement-driven accounts, so this file makes no claim about which carried more.
Sources were retrieved and archive-verified on 2026-08-27; follower counts, engagement figures and page contents decay after that date.
unknowns: Who created and directed the dormant fake-account cohorts Cyabra reported. No public record reviewed here establishes the operator, and platform takedown reports have not (as of retrieval) attributed those specific cohorts.

Whether any actor's internal planning material contains pre-drafted post-attack messaging. Nothing public shows it; absence of evidence in the public record is not evidence of absence, and this file claims only that it is not established.
The full inventory of pre-7 October assets that later carried conflict content. Takedown reports document the networks that were found; they say nothing about networks that were not.

How much post-7 October reach the documented pre-existing networks actually achieved relative to organic spread - Meta assessed Spamouflage as largely failing to reach authentic audiences, while the ad-network and Telegram channels plainly did reach real ones.
contradictions: **Against advance narrative preparation (claim 3) and the coordination inference (claim 4):** Microsoft's threat analysis found Iranian cyber and influence actors *reactive in the initial phase* of the war - re-using dated material from historical operations, exaggerating impact, and operating in the first days in a way *indicating it had little or no coordination with Hamas*. For the state-aligned slice of the ecosystem this is direct counter-evidence to the claim that the response was scripted in advance.

**Against the covert-network framing of the first wave:** NewsGuard's week-one review found 74 percent of the most-viral false or unverified posts on X came from paid-verified accounts - monetized, largely authentic accounts chasing engagement, not pre-built covert infrastructure. The most visible early spread did not need the pre-existing machinery.

**Against a scripted rollout:** ISD's year-scale analysis of 1.8 million posts reads the spread as opportunistic promotion of existing conspiracy repertoires by a diverse set of actors, with major false items traceable to individual influencers misrepresenting mainstream reporting within hours - a dynamic of improvisation on old templates, not execution of a prepared plan.

**On claims 1 and 2 a contradiction was searched for and not found:** no evidence surfaced that Doppelganger, Spamouflage, IUVM or Gaza Now were created after 7 October 2023 or that their pre-war documentation is misdated, and no source disputes that the recycled footage predates the war. Their pre-existence is multiply and independently documented.
wouldChange: Claim 1 (infrastructure) would fall if the pre-war documentation of the named networks were shown to be fabricated or misdated - for example, archive evidence that the 2022 Doppelganger exposure or the August 2023 Spamouflage takedown described assets that did not yet exist. Nothing reviewed points that way.

Claim 2 (recycled material) would fall for any given item if the item were shown to have been first published after 7 October 2023; the claim survives as long as the traced originals genuinely predate the war.

Claim 3 (advance narratives) would flip from not-established to documented if dated primary material surfaced - drafts, scheduled posts, seeded framing or registrations demonstrably created before 7 October 2023 that contain a specific false claim which then circulated after the attack. A platform takedown report or court record with creation timestamps would meet the bar; a retrospective assertion would not.

Claim 4 (speed implies coordination) would rise above inference only if platform-verified data tied the dormant cohorts' creation and activation to an identified operator and showed tasking that predates 7 October - that is, if the coordination itself were documented rather than inferred from timing. Conversely, further platform attribution of week-one spread to authentic engagement-driven accounts would weaken the inference further.

exhibits.statement: The speed at which false content appeared after 7 October 2023 demonstrates that its distribution was coordinated in advance. One vendor reads dormant-account activation as advance preparation; a platform-scale review found the state-aligned response reactive and disorganized in the first days, and a separate week-one review found the most viral false posts came from authentic paid-verified accounts. The coordination reading is an inference from timing, not a documented fact, and the record on it points in more than one direction.

narratives.title: Denial and false-flag reframing
narratives.summary: Claims that the 7 October attack was staged, exaggerated or carried out by Israel itself. The false-flag repertoire long predates 7 October and attached to the event within days.
narratives.frame: A pre-existing conspiracy template applied to a new event; nothing reviewed shows this framing being written for 7 October in advance.
narratives.audience: Conspiracy-adjacent and anti-establishment audiences across platforms

narratives.title: Recycled-footage combat spectacle
narratives.summary: Old conflict footage and video game clips presented as current war video. The old material supplies the imagery; the caption supplies the claim.
narratives.frame: A routine technique with a documented pre-war history, applied to the new conflict immediately.
narratives.audience: General social media audiences during breaking-news windows

narratives.title: State-content laundering
narratives.summary: State outlet messaging republished through sites and accounts that present as independent. Documented for Iranian-aligned networks since 2018; Microsoft documented Iranian influence operations surging in support of Hamas after 7 October.
narratives.frame: Pre-existing laundering channels available to carry conflict messaging once it existed; the channels predate the messaging.
narratives.audience: Western and regional audiences reached through ostensibly independent outlets

Meta announces its largest-ever single takedown against the Spamouflage network, five and a half weeks before 7 October.
Hamas attacks Israel. False and mis-contextualized content begins circulating the same day.
Fact-checkers trace viral combat footage to Arma 3 video game clips and other pre-war material within days of the attack.
Cyabra reports about 40,000 fake pro-Hamas profiles, stating the fake profiles were created beforehand, some over a year earlier, and made active only when the war started.
NewsGuard reports that 74 percent of the most-viral false or unverified week-one posts on X came from paid-verified accounts.

Microsoft's threat analysis finds Iranian cyber and influence actors were reactive in the initial phase of the war, re-using dated material, in a way indicating little or no advance coordination with Hamas.
US and UK authorities sanction the Gaza Now network; the record documents its pre-war existence and its post-attack fundraising for Hamas.
ISD publishes a year-scale analysis of 1.8 million posts on denial and distortion of the 7 October attack, reading the spread as opportunistic reuse of existing conspiracy repertoires.
